questions.question: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT about the Fundamental Rights of the Indian Constitution?

options.text: Cultural and educational rights are fundamental rights.
These are subject to reasonable restriction.
These may be enforced by the courts.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**These are absolute.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution are **not absolute**; they are subject to reasonable restrictions to ensure public order, morality, and national security.
 
• **Article 19(2)** of the Constitution explicitly mentions reasonable restrictions on the freedom of speech and expression.
 
• The Fundamental Rights are enforceable by the courts under **Article 32**, which provides the right to constitutional remedies.
 
• The Constitution grants **Cultural and Educational Rights** as Fundamental Rights under Articles 29 and 30 to protect minority groups.
 
• While Fundamental Rights are guaranteed, they can be suspended during a national emergency as stated under **Article 359**, except for Articles 20 and 21.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights:**

 
 
• These are enshrined in Part III of the Indian Constitution, spanning Articles 12 to 35.
 
• They ensure the basic rights and freedoms of individuals, including equality, freedom, protection against exploitation, and religious freedom.
 
• They are classified into six categories: Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and Right to Constitutional Remedies.
 
 
 
• **Reasonable Restrictions:**
 
 
• Restrictions are imposed to maintain public order, morality, health, security, and friendly relations with foreign states.
 
• Such restrictions are defined within the Constitution and upheld by judicial review to prevent misuse by authorities.
 
 
 
• **Article 32 - Right to Constitutional Remedies:**
 
 
• Referred to as the "heart and soul of the Constitution" by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.
 
• Allows individuals to approach the Supreme Court directly for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
 
• Empowers courts to issue writs such as habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, and certiorari.
 
 
 
• **Suspension of Fundamental Rights:**
 
 
• During a national emergency under Article 352, certain Fundamental Rights can be suspended.
 
• Rights under Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even in emergencies.
 
• Article 358 and Article 359 specify conditions for suspension during emergencies.

questions.question: In which year was the Right to Property removed from the Fundamental Rights of the Constitution of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1978**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Right to Property was originally included as a Fundamental Right under **Article 19(1)(f)** and Article 31 of the Indian Constitution.
 
• It was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights by the **44th Amendment Act, 1978**, during the tenure of Prime Minister Morarji Desai.
 
• After the amendment, the Right to Property was reclassified as a **legal right** under Article 300A in Part XII of the Constitution.
 
• The change was made to resolve conflicts between private property rights and the government's power to acquire land for public purposes.
 
• This amendment curtailed the misuse of property-related rights and allowed the government greater flexibility in enacting land reforms.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights**:

 
 
• These are enshrined in Part III of the Indian Constitution and are justiciable, meaning they can be enforced by courts.
 
• Initially, there were seven Fundamental Rights, but now there are six after the removal of the Right to Property.
 
 
 
• **44th Amendment Act, 1978**:
 
 
• This was enacted to nullify some provisions of the 42nd Amendment, which was passed during the Emergency period (1975-77).
 
• It ensured that Fundamental Rights could not be easily abridged or suspended except during a properly declared emergency.
 
 
 
• **Article 300A**:
 
 
• It states that no person shall be deprived of their property except by the authority of law.
 
• It made the Right to Property a statutory (legal) right instead of a Fundamental Right.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Change**:
 
 
• Reclassification of the Right to Property helped the government implement land acquisition and agrarian reforms more effectively.
 
• It reduced the number of property-related litigations in courts.

questions.question: Which financial institution was established by the 74th Constitutional Amendment, 1992, to review the finances of Urban Local Government Bodies?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**State Finance Commission**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **74th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992** mandated the establishment of the State Finance Commission (SFC) to review the financial position of Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) and Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs).
 
• The SFC is constituted by the respective **State Governments** every five years to recommend measures for improving the financial health of local self-governments.
 
• Its primary responsibility is to **distribute financial resources** between the state government and local bodies, ensuring adequate funding for developmental activities.
 
• The recommendations of the SFC include devolution of taxes, grants-in-aid, and improving revenue-generating capabilities of ULBs and PRIs.
 
• This initiative aligns with the spirit of **decentralization**, empowering local self-governments to perform their functions more effectively.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992**

 
 
• This Act provided a constitutional status to Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) in India.
 
• It introduced the concept of decentralized governance through institutions like Municipalities, Municipal Corporations, and Nagar Panchayats.
 
• It also emphasized the importance of financial sustainability and accountability in local governance.
 
 
 
• **State Finance Commission (SFC)**
 
 
• The SFC was established under Article 243-I of the Constitution.
 
• It is responsible for reviewing the financial position of Panchayati Raj Institutions and Urban Local Bodies within the state.
 
• The SFC provides recommendations on tax assignments, revenue-sharing, and grants-in-aid for local bodies.
 
 
 
• **Urban Local Bodies (ULBs)**
 
 
• ULBs are the governing institutions responsible for administering towns and cities in India.
 
• They include Municipal Corporations, Municipalities, and Nagar Panchayats, which are categorized based on the population size.
 
• ULBs are tasked with providing essential services such as water supply, sanitation, waste management, and urban planning.
 
 
 
• **Decentralization**
 
 
• Decentralization refers to the transfer of decision-making powers and responsibilities from central authorities to lower levels of government.
 
• It aims to improve governance, ensure participation, and enhance service delivery at the grassroots level.
 
• The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments are key milestones in India’s journey toward decentralized governance.

questions.question: Prior to 1992, what was the status of Local Governments in India?

options.text: Directly controlled by the Central Government

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Statutory status under State Law**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Prior to the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments in 1992, Local Governments in India functioned based on **statutory provisions enacted by the respective State Legislatures**.
 
• The Local Government bodies, such as Panchayats and Municipalities, **did not have constitutional recognition** and were established or dissolved at the discretion of state governments.
 
• Local Governments were governed by state-specific laws, resulting in **varying frameworks and powers** across different states.
 
• The absence of constitutional status meant that Local Governments **lacked autonomy** and were primarily dependent on state governments for finances and functional authority.
 
• The 1992 constitutional amendments (73rd and 74th) granted these bodies a **constitutional mandate**, ensuring uniformity, autonomy, and empowerment for self-governance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **73rd Constitutional Amendment Act (1992):**

 
 
• It granted constitutional status to Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs).
 
• Introduced a three-tier system of Panchayats at the village, intermediate, and district levels.
 
• Mandated regular elections, reservation for women and marginalized groups, and the establishment of the State Election Commission.
 
 
 
• **74th Constitutional Amendment Act (1992):**
 
 
• It provided constitutional recognition to Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) such as Municipalities.
 
• Defined the structure, composition, and powers of ULBs to ensure urban self-governance.
 
• Introduced provisions for Metropolitan Planning Committees and District Planning Committees.
 
 
 
• **Statutory Status:**
 
 
• Refers to the status granted to institutions or entities through ordinary legislation passed by a legislative body, such as a State Legislature.
 
• Unlike constitutional status, statutory status can be modified or revoked by amending the enabling legislation.
 
 
 
• **Autonomy of Local Governments Post-1992:**
 
 
• Post-1992, Local Governments gained autonomy in decision-making and financial matters.
 
• They were mandated to prepare plans for economic development and social justice as per the Constitution.

questions.question: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution states about the appointment of the Advocate General for the State?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Article 165**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 165** of the **Indian Constitution** provides for the appointment of the **Advocate General** for the State.
 
• The Advocate General is the **highest law officer** in a state and is responsible for giving advice to the state government on legal matters.
 
• He/she is appointed by the **Governor of the State** and holds office during the pleasure of the Governor.
 
• The Advocate General must be a person qualified to be appointed as a **Judge of a High Court**, which means he/she should have been an advocate of a High Court for at least **10 years** or should have held a judicial office for a similar period.
 
• The duties of the Advocate General include:
 
 
• Giving advice on legal matters to the **state government**.
 
• Performing legal duties assigned by the **Governor**.
 
• Representing the state government in the **High Court** or the **Supreme Court** in cases where the state is a party.
 
 
 
• The Advocate General has the **right to speak** and take part in the proceedings of the state legislature, but he/she does not have the right to vote.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 164**__

 __
 
• **Article 164** of the Constitution pertains to the **appointment of Chief Ministers and other Ministers** for the state by the Governor.
 
• It also mentions the **collective responsibility** of the Council of Ministers to the state legislature.
 
 
 
• **Article 162**__
 __
 
• **Article 162** defines the **extent of executive power** of the state government.
 
• It states that the executive power of the state extends to matters on which the state legislature has the power to make laws.
 
 
 
• **Article 163**__
 
 
• **Article 163** deals with the **Council of Ministers** to aid and advise the Governor of a state.
 
• The Governor is required to act according to the **advice of the Council of Ministers**, except in cases where the Constitution requires him to act at his discretion.

questions.question: Which of the following disputes is excluded from the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court?

options.text: A commercial contract dispute between Gujarat and a private company
A disagreement between Punjab and Haryana over territorial boundaries
A dispute between Maharashtra and the Centre over a constitutional law issue
A dispute between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu over water sharing

questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**A dispute between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu over water sharing**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **original jurisdiction** of the Supreme Court in India is defined under **Article 131** of the Indian Constitution.
 
• This jurisdiction allows the Supreme Court to adjudicate disputes between:
 
 
• **The Government of India and one or more States**
 
• **Between two or more States**
 
 
 
• However, disputes related to **water sharing** between states are excluded from the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.
 
• Such disputes are governed by the **Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956**, and are handled by **water tribunals**, not the Supreme Court.
 
• The water-sharing dispute between **Karnataka and Tamil Nadu** is primarily related to the **Cauvery River**, which has been a long-standing issue.
 
• These disputes are resolved through dedicated mechanisms such as the **Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal** rather than the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **A commercial contract dispute between Gujarat and a private company**__

 __
 
• Such disputes typically fall under the jurisdiction of **civil courts** or specialized tribunals, depending on the nature of the contract.
 
• They do not qualify as disputes between states or the central government under **Article 131**.
 
 
 
• **A disagreement between Punjab and Haryana over territorial boundaries**__
 __
 
• Disputes over **territorial boundaries** between states fall under the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.
 
• For example, boundary disputes can arise due to historical treaties or administrative decisions.
 
 
 
• **A dispute between Maharashtra and the Centre over a constitutional law issue**__
 
 
• Constitutional law issues between states and the central government fall under the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction as defined in **Article 131**.
 
• Such issues typically involve interpretations of the Constitution or implementation of central laws.

questions.question: Under which provision can the Governor extend judicial service rules to certain magistrates?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Article 237**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 237** of the Indian Constitution empowers the Governor to extend the provisions relating to the conditions of service of judicial officers to certain magistrates.
 
• This article allows the **Governor** to declare that the provisions of Part VI, Chapter VI of the Constitution (dealing with subordinate courts) shall apply to any magistrate or judicial officer.
 
• The provisions are intended to ensure that judicial services are uniform and consistent across the country.
 
• This enables administrative and procedural improvements in the functioning of magistrates, ensuring they conform to judicial standards.
 
• The decision under Article 237 allows for better integration of **judicial services** into the wider legal framework of the Constitution.
 
• It is significant for maintaining **judicial independence** and ensuring fair administration of justice.
 
• Article 237 is part of the broader constitutional framework aimed at enhancing the efficiency and accountability of judicial officers.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 233**__

 __
 
• **Article 233** deals with the appointment of District Judges.
 
• It specifies that appointments, posting, and promotions of District Judges are made by the Governor of the state in consultation with the High Court.
 
• This article ensures judicial independence by involving the judiciary in the appointment process.
 
 
 
• **Article 142**__
 __
 
• **Article 142** empowers the Supreme Court of India to pass any decree or order necessary for doing complete justice in any matter.
 
• This article is used as a tool for judicial activism, enabling the Supreme Court to deliver justice in extraordinary circumstances.
 
• It is often invoked for enforcing orders that go beyond the limits of statutory law.
 
 
 
• **Article 234**__
 
 
• **Article 234** deals with the recruitment of persons to the judicial service other than District Judges.
 
• It specifies that such appointments are made by the Governor of the state in consultation with the State Public Service Commission and the High Court.
 
• This ensures proper procedures in the recruitment process for subordinate judicial officers.

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution of India provides a right to profess, practice and propagate religion?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 25**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 25** of the Indian Constitution guarantees all individuals the freedom of conscience and the right to freely profess, practice, and propagate religion.
 
• This article is part of the **Fundamental Rights** under Part III of the Constitution, specifically ensuring religious freedom.
 
• The rights under Article 25 are subject to public order, morality, and health, and other provisions of Part III.
 
• It applies equally to all persons, irrespective of their religion, ensuring secularism as a core principle of the Indian Constitution.
 
• Article 25 also allows the state to regulate or restrict any economic, financial, political, or other secular activities associated with religious practices.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 26:** Provides the right to manage religious affairs, allowing religious denominations to establish institutions for religious and charitable purposes.
 
• **Article 27:** Prohibits compelling any person to pay taxes for the promotion or maintenance of any religion or religious institutions.
 
• **Article 28:** Addresses freedom as to attendance at religious instruction or religious worship in certain educational institutions.
 
• **Secularism in India:** Indian secularism guarantees the state’s neutrality towards all religions while allowing freedom of religious practices.
 
• **Restrictions on Article 25:** The state can intervene to regulate practices that contradict public order, morality, or health, or for social welfare reforms such as the abolition of untouchability or sati.

questions.question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution empowers Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 11**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 11** of the Indian Constitution empowers the Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship through legislation.
 
• It allows the Parliament to make laws concerning the acquisition, termination, and other matters related to citizenship.
 
• This article is part of Part II (Articles 5 to 11) of the Constitution, which deals with Citizenship.
 
• Using the powers under Article 11, the Parliament has enacted laws like the **Citizenship Act of 1955** and its subsequent amendments.
 
• While Articles 5 to 10 determine the citizenship status of individuals at the commencement of the Constitution, Article 11 enables future legislative actions on citizenship matters.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Part II of the Constitution:** It deals with the provisions related to citizenship from Articles 5 to 11.
 
• **Citizenship Act of 1955:** This law, enacted under Article 11, specifies the methods for acquiring, losing, and determining Indian citizenship.
 
• **Modes of Acquiring Citizenship:** The Citizenship Act provides five modes: by birth, descent, registration, naturalization, and incorporation of territory.
 
• **Amendments to Citizenship Act:** Significant amendments include the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019, which introduced provisions for granting citizenship to certain persecuted minorities from neighboring countries.
 
• **Difference Between Articles 5-10 and Article 11:** Articles 5-10 primarily address citizenship at the time of the Constitution's commencement, while Article 11 grants the Parliament the power to legislate on citizenship matters post-constitution.

questions.question: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution states about the duty of Union Public Service Commission to present its report annually to the President of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is ​__**Article 323**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 323** of the Indian Constitution describes the duty of the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) to present its annual report to the President of India.
 
• The President places this report before both Houses of Parliament, along with a memorandum explaining cases where the Commission's advice was not accepted.
 
• This provision ensures the accountability and transparency of the UPSC's functioning.
 
• The Union Public Service Commission is a constitutional body established under Part XIV of the Indian Constitution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Union Public Service Commission (UPSC)**

 
 
• It is responsible for conducting examinations for appointments to civil services and posts under the Union Government.
 
• UPSC is one of the central recruiting agencies of India, established under Article 315 of the Constitution.
 
• The Commission consists of a chairman and other members appointed by the President of India.
 
• It functions independently to ensure unbiased recruitment for civil service positions.
 
 
 
• **Constitutional Articles Related to UPSC**
 
 
• **Article 315:** Establishment of Public Service Commissions for the Union and States.
 
• **Article 316:** Appointment and term of office of members of the UPSC.
 
• **Article 317:** Removal and suspension of members of Public Service Commissions.
 
• **Article 323:** Reports of the UPSC and their presentation to the President.
 
 
 
• **Role of UPSC**
 
 
• Conducting examinations such as the Civil Services Examination (CSE), Engineering Services Examination (ESE), and others.
 
• Advising the government on matters related to recruitment, promotions, and disciplinary actions.
 
• Ensuring merit-based selection for appointments in public services.

questions.question: In the three-tier structure of the Panchayati Raj system in India, which body is elected at the grassroots level?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gram Panchayat**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Gram Panchayat** is the grassroots-level body in the three-tier Panchayati Raj system in India.
 
• It is directly elected by the people of the village, forming the first tier of the Panchayati Raj system.
 
• The Gram Panchayat is responsible for local governance and development activities in villages.
 
• Its members are elected for a term of **five years** by the eligible voters in the village.
 
• The head of the Gram Panchayat is called the **Sarpanch**, who is also elected by the villagers.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Panchayati Raj System in India:**

 
 
• The Panchayati Raj system is a decentralized form of governance in which gram panchayats are the basic units of administration.
 
• It was constitutionalized through the **73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992**.
 
• The system has three levels: Gram Panchayat (village level), Panchayat Samiti (block level), and Zila Parishad (district level).
 
 
 
• **Roles and Responsibilities of Gram Panchayat:**
 
 
• Implementation of development programs such as rural housing, sanitation, and drinking water supply.
 
• Maintenance of public assets like roads, schools, and community centers.
 
• Promotion of literacy, health, and awareness programs in rural areas.
 
 
 
• **Funding of Gram Panchayats:**
 
 
• Funds are provided through **grants from the central and state governments**, revenue generated locally, and other sources.
 
• The Finance Commission recommends financial allocations to Panchayati Raj institutions.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Grassroots Governance:**
 
 
• It ensures that governance is **inclusive** and caters to the specific needs of rural populations.
 
• It encourages local participation in decision-making and promotes accountability.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an elected position under the Panchayati Raj system in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Panchayat Secretary**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Panchayat Secretary** is not an elected position under the Panchayati Raj system; it is an appointed administrative role.
 
• The Panchayat Secretary is usually appointed by the **state government** to assist in the functioning and administration of the Panchayat.
 
• This role primarily involves record-keeping, maintaining accounts, and implementing government schemes at the Panchayat level.
 
• In contrast, positions like **Sarpanch, Zila Pramukh, and Pradhan** are elected by the people under the democratic framework of the Panchayati Raj system.
 
• The Panchayat Secretary acts as a link between the elected representatives and the state government for administrative purposes.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Panchayati Raj System**

 
 
• The Panchayati Raj is a three-tier system of local self-governance in India, consisting of Gram Panchayat (village level), Block Samiti (block level), and Zila Parishad (district level).
 
• It was introduced through the **73rd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992**.
 
• The system aims to empower rural areas with self-governance and decentralized administration.
 
• Each tier has elected representatives, ensuring grassroots democracy.
 
 
 
• **Key Elected Positions in Panchayati Raj**
 
 
• **Sarpanch:** Head of the Gram Panchayat, elected by the villagers.
 
• **Pradhan:** Chairperson of the Panchayat Samiti at the block level.
 
• **Zila Pramukh:** Head of the Zila Parishad, elected by the members of the Parishad.
 
 
 
• **Roles of Panchayat Secretary**
 
 
• Maintains records of meetings, resolutions, and accounts.
 
• Coordinates the implementation of government schemes and programs.
 
• Acts as a liaison between the Panchayat and state or district administration.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Panchayati Raj**
 
 
• Promotes participatory governance and decision-making at the grassroots level.
 
• Ensures the delivery of basic services like water supply, sanitation, and rural development schemes.
 
• Empowers marginalized groups, including women and Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes, through mandatory reservation of seats.

questions.question: In the 2024 Jharkhand Assembly elections, how many seats were won by the winning party/coalition and what is the name of the party/coalition?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**56 seats, JMM-led alliance INDIA**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The JMM-led alliance INDIA secured a total of **56 seats** in the 2024 Jharkhand Assembly elections, ensuring a majority in the 81-member Assembly.
 
• The alliance was composed of the Jharkhand Mukti Morcha (JMM), Indian National Congress (INC), and Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD), among others.
 
• The JMM, under the leadership of Chief Minister Hemant Soren, played a pivotal role in consolidating votes from tribal and rural regions of the state.

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution of India provides guidelines for states to make laws on the protection of monuments and objects of national importance?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Article 49**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 49** of the **Indian Constitution** falls under the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP).
 
• It directs the **State** to ensure the protection of every **monument or place or object** of artistic or historic interest that is of national importance.
 
• This Article emphasizes that such monuments or objects should not be **spoliated, disfigured, destroyed, removed, disposed of, or exported.**
 
• The **objective** of this Article is to preserve and maintain the rich cultural heritage of India for future generations.
 
• This provision is part of the **Directive Principles of State Policy**, meaning it is not enforceable by the courts but provides important guidelines for the government.
 
• It reinforces the government's responsibility to promote and protect India's **artistic, cultural, and historical legacy.**
 
• The protection of monuments is also supplemented by laws such as the **Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 48**__

 __
 
• It directs the State to organize agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines.
 
• It also promotes the preservation and improvement of breeds and prohibits the slaughter of cows, calves, and other milch and draught cattle.
 
 
 
• **Article 50**__
 __
 
• This Article mandates the separation of the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.
 
• It aims to ensure judicial independence and the rule of law.
 
 
 
• **Article 48A**__
 
 
• Added by the **42nd Amendment Act, 1976**, it directs the State to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife.
 
• It highlights the importance of environmental conservation as part of the Directive Principles.

questions.question: Which of the following provisions are covered under Article 4 of the Constitution of India?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Laws for reorganisation of states**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Article 4** of the **Indian Constitution** deals specifically with the **reorganisation of states** and the related laws.
 
• It states that any laws enacted under **Article 2 (admission or establishment of new states)** or **Article 3 (formation of new states and alteration of areas, boundaries, or names of existing states)** are not considered amendments to the Constitution

questions.question: Which position within the Union Council of Ministers of India is immediately below the Prime Minister in hierarchy?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Cabinet Minister**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Union Council of Ministers** in India consists of different levels of ministers, including the Prime Minister, **Cabinet Ministers**, Ministers of State, and Deputy Ministers.
 
• A **Cabinet Minister** holds the highest position in the council after the Prime Minister and is responsible for major ministries such as Finance, Defence, Home Affairs, External Affairs, etc.
 
• Cabinet Ministers are part of the **core decision-making body** in the government and attend cabinet meetings chaired by the Prime Minister.
 
• The Cabinet Ministers are responsible for framing policies, implementing laws, and overseeing the functioning of their respective ministries.
 
• The hierarchy within the Union Council of Ministers places the **Cabinet Minister** immediately below the Prime Minister, followed by Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers.
 
• This structure ensures efficient governance and delegation of responsibilities across various levels of the government.
 
• Cabinet Ministers are appointed by the **President of India** on the advice of the Prime Minister.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Minister of State**__

 __
 
• A **Minister of State** is a junior minister who assists the Cabinet Minister in handling their respective ministry.
 
• They may handle specific responsibilities within the ministry or act as independent ministers for less critical portfolios.
 
• While they attend meetings and contribute to policy discussions, they are not part of the core Cabinet meetings.
 
 
 
• **Deputy Minister**__
 __
 
• **Deputy Ministers** are at a lower rank compared to Ministers of State and mainly assist in administrative and operational tasks.
 
• They do not have independent portfolios and work under the guidance of senior ministers.
 
 
 
• **Parliamentary Secretary**__
 
 
• A **Parliamentary Secretary** is not considered a minister but acts as an aide to a senior minister or Cabinet Minister.
 
• They focus on legislative duties and help coordinate between the ministry and parliament.

questions.question: Under its original jurisdiction, the Supreme Court of India can adjudicate disputes between:

options.text: The Centre and one or more states
Two private citizens from different states
Two municipal corporations of different states
A state government and a private corporation

questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**The Centre and one or more states**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **original jurisdiction** of the Supreme Court of India is defined under **Article 131** of the Indian Constitution.
 
• In its original jurisdiction, the Supreme Court can adjudicate disputes between the **Government of India (Centre) and one or more states**.
 
• This jurisdiction is exclusive to the Supreme Court, meaning no other court in India can handle such disputes.
 
• It also includes disputes between **two or more states**, or between the Centre and any state(s) on one side and other states on the other side.
 
• This ensures the maintenance of a **federal balance** and resolves any legal conflicts that may arise between different levels of government.
 
• However, it is important to note that this jurisdiction is limited to **questions of law** or **questions of fact** on which the existence of a legal right depends.
 
• Some examples of cases under this jurisdiction include disputes related to **taxation, water disputes, or constitutional interpretation.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Two private citizens from different states**__

 __
 
• Disputes between private citizens are not within the **original jurisdiction** of the Supreme Court.
 
• Such matters are generally dealt with by **civil courts** or **high courts** in India.
 
 
 
• **Two municipal corporations of different states**__
 __
 
• Municipal corporations are governed by their respective state governments, and any disputes between them would not fall under the **original jurisdiction** of the Supreme Court.
 
• Such cases would typically be resolved within the jurisdiction of the respective **state high courts**.
 
 
 
• **A state government and a private corporation**__
 
 
• Disputes involving private corporations are not covered under Article 131.
 
• Such matters are generally resolved through **civil courts** or other legal mechanisms, including tribunals.

questions.question: What is the term for elected members serving on the board of a co-operative society?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**5 years**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The tenure of **elected members** serving on the board of a **co-operative society** is generally prescribed under the respective **State Co-operative Societies Acts** or the **Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act** (for multi-state societies).
 
• As per the **Indian Co-operative Societies Act**, the elected members of the board typically serve for a term of **5 years**.
 
• This ensures a balance between **continuity of governance** and the opportunity for members to bring in new leadership or policy direction.
 
• The **5-year term** allows boards to implement long-term plans and strategies effectively for the betterment of the society and its members.
 
• The election process for board members is conducted in a **democratic manner**, ensuring representation and fairness for all members of the co-operative society.
 
• In certain cases, the tenure can vary depending on the **specific state laws or bylaws** of the co-operative society, but 5 years remains the standard term.
 
• The governance system in co-operative societies emphasizes transparency, accountability, and **member participation**, aligning with their democratic principles.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **3 years**

 
 
• The **3-year term** is not standard for co-operative societies in India. However, some organizations or committees with shorter project timelines may adopt this tenure.
 
• In certain countries, the tenure for elected members in similar entities might be 3 years, but this is not typically applicable to Indian co-operative societies.
 
 
 
• **4 years**
 
 
• A **4-year term** is more commonly seen in corporate governance or public office elections in some countries, but it is not a standard tenure for co-operative society boards in India.
 
 
 
• **6 years**
 
 
• A **6-year term** is generally considered too long for elected positions in co-operative societies, as it might hinder the democratic principle of allowing members to elect new representatives periodically.
 
• It is uncommon for co-operative societies in India to have a tenure of 6 years for board members.

questions.question: How many writs mentioned in the Constitution of India enforce Fundamental Rights?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Five Writs**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The Constitution of India empowers the **Supreme Court (under Article 32)** and the **High Courts (under Article 226)** to issue five types of writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
 
• The five writs mentioned in the Constitution are:
 
 
• **Habeas Corpus:** A writ to produce a person detained or imprisoned before the court to examine the legality of their detention.
 
• **Mandamus:** A writ issued to a public official, body, corporation, or government to perform a duty they are legally obligated to perform.
 
• **Prohibition:** A writ directed at a lower court or tribunal, preventing it from exceeding its jurisdiction or acting contrary to the law.
 
• **Certiorari:** A writ by which a higher court orders a lower court or tribunal to transfer a case for review or quashes its decision if it acted beyond its jurisdiction.
 
• **Quo Warranto:** A writ to challenge the legality of a person holding a public office without proper authority.
 
 
 
• These writs are significant tools to ensure the protection of **Fundamental Rights** under Part III of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The Supreme Court's power to issue writs is primarily for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights, making it a guardian of these rights.
 
• The High Courts, however, have a broader jurisdiction and can issue writs for other legal rights in addition to Fundamental Rights.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Four Writs**__

 __
 
• The concept of issuing writs is derived from the **English Common Law**, which initially included only four primary writs. However, the Indian Constitution explicitly mentions five writs.
 
• Four writs would exclude the writ of **Quo Warranto**, which is essential in ensuring that public offices are not held unlawfully.
 
 
 
• **Six Writs**__
 __
 
• The Indian Constitution does not mention six writs. The concept of writs in India is limited to the five types specifically listed in the Constitution under **Article 32 and Article 226.**
 
 
 
• **Seven Writs**__
 
 
• The Constitution of India does not authorize the issuance of seven writs. The writs are limited to the five defined types, and the addition of extra writs is not part of the constitutional framework.

questions.question: Which of the following writs protects the right to life and personal liberty mentioned in the Constitution of India?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Habeas Corpus**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The writ of **Habeas Corpus** is one of the most important writs used to protect the **right to life and personal liberty** as guaranteed under **Article 21** of the **Indian Constitution**.
 
• The term **Habeas Corpus** means "you may have the body." It is a judicial mandate to produce a person who has been detained or imprisoned before the court to determine the legality of their detention.
 
• This writ ensures that no individual is deprived of their **fundamental rights** arbitrarily and is a safeguard against unlawful detention.
 
• The court can order the release of the detained person if it finds that the detention was done without legal justification.
 
• This writ can be filed by the detained person themselves or by someone on their behalf.
 
• The writ of **Habeas Corpus** is applicable in cases of both **preventive detention** and **illegal detention**.
 
• The right to file this writ can be enforced against both **public authorities** and **private individuals**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mandamus**__

 __
 
• The writ of **Mandamus** means "we command." It is issued by a court to direct a **public official**, **government authority**, or **lower court** to perform a duty they are obligated to perform.
 
• It cannot be issued against a private individual or organization.
 
• The writ of Mandamus is mostly used to ensure the proper functioning of authorities as per the law.
 
 
 
• **Certiorari**__
 __
 
• The writ of **Certiorari** is issued to a lower court or tribunal to transfer a case to a higher authority or to quash an order passed by the lower court if it acted beyond its jurisdiction.
 
• This writ ensures judicial oversight and prevents the misuse of power by lower courts.
 
 
 
• **Prohibition**__
 
 
• The writ of **Prohibition** is issued by a higher court to a lower court or tribunal, directing it to stop proceedings in a case where it lacks jurisdiction.
 
• It is a preventive writ used to prevent an overreach of authority or jurisdiction.

questions.question: Which of the following groups is NOT considered a part of the Union Council of Ministers in India?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Parliamentary Secretaries**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Union Council of Ministers** in India is a constitutional body established under **Article 74 and Article 75** of the Constitution of India.
 
• The Council of Ministers consists of **Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State (with or without independent charge), and Deputy Ministers**.
 
• **Parliamentary Secretaries** are not considered a part of the Union Council of Ministers as their role is not defined under the Constitution of India.
 
• Parliamentary Secretaries are appointed to assist ministers, but they do not hold a formal ministerial position or have executive powers.
 
• Their role is often advisory, and they act as a link between the minister and the Parliament.
 
• In some cases, the appointment of Parliamentary Secretaries has been a subject of legal and constitutional challenges due to the **office of profit** clause under **Article 102(1)(a)** and **Article 191(1)(a)** of the Constitution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Deputy Ministers**__

 __
 
• **Deputy Ministers** are part of the Union Council of Ministers and assist the Cabinet Ministers or Ministers of State in their respective departments.
 
• They are subordinate to the Cabinet Ministers and do not hold independent charge of a ministry.
 
• Their primary role is to handle specific responsibilities assigned by their superiors.
 
 
 
• **Ministers of State**__
 __
 
• **Ministers of State** can either hold independent charge of a ministry or assist a Cabinet Minister in managing the workload of a specific ministry.
 
• When holding independent charge, they perform functions similar to Cabinet Ministers but are ranked lower in hierarchy.
 
• They are an important part of the Union Council of Ministers.
 
 
 
• **Cabinet Ministers**__
 
 
• **Cabinet Ministers** are the senior-most members of the Union Council of Ministers.
 
• They hold independent charge of major ministries like **Home Affairs, Finance, Defence, and External Affairs**.
 
• They play a key role in decision-making and policy formulation within the government.
 
• The Cabinet is collectively responsible to the **Lok Sabha** as per **Article 75(3)** of the Constitution.

questions.question: Which of the following options correctly describes the Indian President’s power to summon the Parliament?

options.text: The President may summon the Parliament only once every calendar year.
The President may summon the Parliament at least twice a year.
The President can only summon the Parliament after consulting the Prime Minister.
The President may summon the Parliament at his/her discretion with no statutory minimum frequency.

questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**The President may summon the Parliament at least twice a year.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Under **Article 85 of the Indian Constitution**, the President has the power to summon the Parliament.
 
• The Constitution mandates that there should not be a gap of more than **six months** between two sessions of Parliament.
 
• This ensures that the Parliament convenes at least **twice every year**.
 
• The summoning of Parliament is done on the advice of the **Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister**.
 
• The sessions of Parliament include the **Budget Session** (February-March), **Monsoon Session** (July-August), and **Winter Session** (November-December).
 
• Summoning the Parliament is an important aspect of the President's role in ensuring the functioning of the **legislative process** in India.
 
• This provision is aimed at maintaining the democratic functioning of the government and its accountability to the Parliament.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **The President may summon the Parliament only once every calendar year**__

 __
 
• This option is incorrect as it violates the provisions of **Article 85**, which states that the Parliament must convene at least twice a year.
 
 
 
• **The President can only summon the Parliament after consulting the Prime Minister**__
 __
 
• While the President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister, the term "consulting" is misleading.
 
• In reality, the President does not act independently but follows the advice given by the **Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers**.
 
 
 
• **The President may summon the Parliament at his/her discretion with no statutory minimum frequency**__
 
 
• This option is incorrect because the summoning of Parliament is governed by **constitutional provisions** under Article 85, which mandates a minimum frequency.
 
• The President does not have complete discretion in this regard; the process is regulated by the Constitution and requires adherence to its provisions.

questions.question: Under which Act was the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA), which conducts Lok Adalats along with other Legal Services Institutions, constituted?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **National Legal Services Authority (NALSA)** was constituted under the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**.
 
• The primary aim of NALSA is to ensure **free legal aid** to weaker sections of society and promote justice on the basis of equal opportunity.
 
• It works to organize **Lok Adalats**, which are informal courts that resolve disputes through conciliation and settlement.
 
• The Act emphasizes providing **legal services** to marginalized groups such as women, children, Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and other vulnerable communities.
 
• Under this Act, **State Legal Services Authorities** were also created to implement policies and organize legal aid programs at the state level.
 
• It is an important law for ensuring compliance with **Article 39A** of the Indian Constitution, which mandates free legal aid to economically weaker sections and promotes equality before the law.
 
• The Act also empowers NALSA to conduct **legal awareness campaigns** to educate citizens about their rights and duties.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Public Interest Litigation Act, 1990**__

 __
 
• There is no specific law called the **Public Interest Litigation Act, 1990**. Public Interest Litigation (PIL) refers to a judicial process under which cases can be filed for protecting public interests.
 
• PILs are governed by various provisions of the **Indian Constitution**, especially **Articles 32 and 226**, which allow individuals to approach the Supreme Court or High Courts.
 
• This concept was introduced in the 1980s and is not linked to a specific act but rather to judicial activism.
 
 
 
• **Advocates Act, 1961**__
 __
 
• The **Advocates Act, 1961** governs the legal profession in India and provides for the establishment of the **Bar Council of India** and State Bar Councils.
 
• It regulates the standards of professional conduct, etiquette, and legal education for advocates.
 
• This Act focuses on the administration and organization of the legal profession rather than providing legal aid services.
 
 
 
• **Indian Bar Council Act, 1926**__
 
 
• The **Indian Bar Council Act, 1926** was enacted to provide for the establishment of Bar Councils in different provinces and regulate the legal profession.
 
• It was a precursor to the **Advocates Act, 1961** and laid the foundation for the legal profession in India.
 
• This Act does not deal with legal aid or the organization of Lok Adalats.

questions.question: The Sixth Schedule of the Indian Constitution deals with the administration of tribal areas in which region?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 1,

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Sixth Schedule of the Indian Constitution provides for special administrative arrangements for tribal areas in the states of **Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram** located in North-East India.
 
• It establishes **Autonomous District Councils (ADCs)**, which are empowered to manage local governance, resource management, and cultural preservation in tribal regions.
 
• The ADCs under the Sixth Schedule have legislative, judicial, and executive powers to ensure tribal self-governance.
 
• The Schedule aims to protect tribal identity and autonomy while ensuring their integration into India's political framework.
 
• It allows tribal communities to enact laws on subjects like land, forests, and social customs, enabling the safeguarding of their unique heritage.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Tribal Areas in India**

 
 
• India recognizes tribal areas under the Fifth and Sixth Schedules of the Constitution.
 
• Fifth Schedule deals with tribal areas outside the North-East, while Sixth Schedule applies exclusively to North-East India.
 
 
 
• **Autonomous District Councils (ADCs)**
 
 
• ADCs are constitutionally established bodies under the Sixth Schedule.
 
• They have the authority to legislate on matters such as land use, resource management, and cultural practices.
 
• The councils aim to preserve tribal autonomy and manage development activities in tribal areas.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Sixth Schedule**
 
 
• It ensures the preservation of tribal identity and culture.
 
• Empowers tribal groups to govern themselves and manage their resources.
 
• Balances autonomy with integration into the national governance framework.
 
 
 
• **States Covered Under Sixth Schedule**
 
 
• Currently, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram are included under the Sixth Schedule.
 
• These states have multiple tribal communities with unique cultural and social practices.

questions.question: Which Schedule and Article contain the names and extent of states and union territories?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**First Schedule – Articles 1 and 4**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **First Schedule** of the Indian Constitution contains the **names and territorial extent of States and Union Territories**.
 
• It is referenced in **Articles 1 and 4** of the Constitution.
 
• Article 1 declares India as a "Union of States" and provides for the classification of its territories into states, union territories, and other areas.
 
• Article 4 specifies the legislative process for changes in the names, boundaries, or formation of States and Union Territories, linking directly to the First Schedule.
 
• The First Schedule is periodically updated to reflect changes in state boundaries or new additions (e.g., Telangana in 2014).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 1 of the Constitution:**

 
 
• Defines India as a "Union of States."
 
• Describes the classification of territories into States, Union Territories, and other areas.
 
 
 
• **Article 4 of the Constitution:**
 
 
• Empowers Parliament to make laws for the admission or establishment of new States or altering the boundaries of existing States.
 
• Such laws are not considered constitutional amendments under Article 368.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the First Schedule:**
 
 
• It provides the official names and territorial descriptions of all States and Union Territories.
 
• It is amended whenever there are changes in state boundaries (e.g., creation of new States like Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, and Jharkhand in 2000).
 
 
 
• **Examples of Amendments:**
 
 
• The Andhra Pradesh Reorganization Act, 2014, led to the creation of Telangana, updating the First Schedule.
 
• Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh were added as Union Territories under the Jammu & Kashmir Reorganization Act, 2019.

questions.question: When did the citizenship provisions in the Constitution come into effect?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 2,

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The citizenship provisions as outlined in Part II of the Indian Constitution came into effect on **November 26, 1949**, coinciding with the enforcement of the Constitution of India.
 
• January 26, 1950, is celebrated as **Republic Day** in India, marking the transition of India into a sovereign democratic republic.
 
• Article 5 to Article 11 in the Constitution of India specifically deals with citizenship provisions at the time of commencement of the Constitution.
 
• The provision for citizenship was crucial for determining the legal status of individuals residing in India after independence and partition.
 
• The Constitution provides for a single citizenship for the entire country, which means that all Indians are citizens of India irrespective of the state or territory they reside in.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 5:** Defines citizenship for individuals domiciled in India at the commencement of the Constitution.
 
• **Article 6:** Grants citizenship to individuals who migrated to India from Pakistan before July 19, 1948, under specific conditions.
 
• **Article 7:** Provides citizenship for individuals who migrated to Pakistan but later returned to India under a permit for resettlement.
 
• **Article 9:** States that individuals voluntarily acquiring citizenship of another country will cease to be Indian citizens.
 
• **Article 10:** Empowers Parliament to regulate citizenship matters through legislation, leading to the enactment of the Citizenship Act, 1955.
 
• **Citizenship Act, 1955:** This act defines provisions for acquiring, terminating, and determining Indian citizenship post-1950.

questions.question: Which type of legislative bills must be introduced in the Lok Sabha only after obtaining the prior approval of the President of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 4,

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Money Bills** must be introduced in the Lok Sabha exclusively, as per Article 110 of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The prior approval of the President of India is mandatory for the introduction of Money Bills in the Lok Sabha.
 
• Money Bills include provisions related to taxation, borrowing of money, expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India, and other financial matters.
 
• The Speaker of the Lok Sabha holds the authority to certify whether a bill is a Money Bill or not.
 
• The Rajya Sabha can only recommend amendments to Money Bills but cannot reject or amend them directly; the Lok Sabha has the final say.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 110:** Defines Money Bills and specifies the matters it can include, such as imposition, abolition, or alteration of taxes, regulation of borrowing, and appropriation of funds.
 
• **Difference between Money Bills and Financial Bills:** Financial Bills deal with broader financial matters but are not exclusively categorized under Article 110, requiring a different legislative process.
 
• **Role of the President:** The President’s recommendation is essential for Money Bills because they involve financial implications for the government.
 
• **Speaker's Certification:** The Speaker of the Lok Sabha’s certification is conclusive and cannot be questioned in any court of law.
 
• **Rajya Sabha's Role:** The Rajya Sabha has limited authority over Money Bills and can only recommend changes within a 14-day window, which the Lok Sabha may accept or reject.
